# Results — Study 895 (Defensive Momentum)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test —
**"momentum without the crashes": a 50/50 (or inverse-vol) blend of MTUM (momentum) and
USMV (min-vol) should deliver a higher excess-of-cash Sharpe and shallower momentum-crash
drawdowns than MTUM alone, net of costs** — audited on monthly total returns vs each
sleeve, QUAL and SPY. Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py`
to reproduce every number. Data as-of 2026-06-30 (monthly stats sliced to the last complete
calendar month; the partial current month is dropped). Fingerprint `7d4dcacd42bd`.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily auto-adjusted closes (**total return**, dividends reinvested, net of fees) — MTUM, USMV, QUAL, SPY, **BIL** (1-3M T-bill ETF = the cash leg; its own total return IS the monthly risk-free rate) |
| Blend window | both sleeves exist from **MTUM's 2013-05 inception** → 2026-06 = **158 months** (USMV alone runs to 176m, SPY to 233m — the blend is MTUM-inception-limited) |
| Excess-of-cash | every Sharpe and race is computed on returns **minus BIL** (both legs excess-of-cash) |
| Rebalance / costs | 50/50 monthly-rebalanced; inverse-vol weights formed on trailing-12m realized vol known at the **end of month *t−1*** and applied to month *t* (one month of lag, no look-ahead). Net = gross − one-way cost × realized turnover; the blend is **long-only** (no borrow leg) |

> **Short history — named on the Signal axis.** MTUM the ETF launched **2013-04**, so the
> canonical **2008-09 momentum crash** the whole "defensive momentum" thesis is built on is
> **entirely out of this sample**. The only equity-momentum sell-offs on the tape are the
> **2020 COVID** crash and the **2022** bear (plus the 2018-Q4 wobble). Thirteen years of
> one wrapper is a short, bull-heavy window; the numbers below describe *this* tape, not the
> century of factor history the pitch invokes.

## Per-strategy stats (same 158-month window; excess = minus BIL cash)

| strategy | CAGR | ann vol | excess Sharpe | max DD | growth of $1 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **MTUM** (momentum) | 16.80% | 16.3% | **0.941** | −30.2% | 7.72 |
| **USMV** (min-vol) | 10.40% | 11.5% | 0.775 | −19.1% | 3.68 |
| **QUAL** (quality) | 13.75% | 14.7% | 0.841 | −27.8% | 5.28 |
| **SPY** (market) | 14.38% | 14.4% | 0.895 | −23.9% | 5.86 |
| **50/50 blend** (gross) | 13.70% | 13.1% | **0.924** | −22.2% | 5.42 |
| **50/50 blend** (net, 3bps/side) | 13.69% | 13.1% | 0.924 | −22.2% | 5.42 |
| **inverse-vol blend** (gross) | 12.98% | 12.9% | 0.875 | −21.9% | 4.41 |
| **inverse-vol blend** (net) | 12.96% | 12.9% | 0.874 | −21.9% | 4.41 |

The blend's Sharpe (**0.924**) sits *between* its two sleeves (USMV 0.775, MTUM 0.941) —
essentially **on the line** joining them. There is **no convexity / free-lunch lift**: you
buy lower volatility (13.1% vs 16.3%) and a shallower full-window drawdown (−22% vs −30%),
and you pay for it almost exactly 1-for-1 in return (CAGR 13.7% vs 16.8%).

## Headline — the excess-vs-excess Sharpe race: does the blend beat MTUM alone?

Both legs excess-of-cash; the **Sharpe advantage** of the blend over MTUM, the **Newey-West
*t*** on the monthly return difference, and a 2,000-draw moving-block bootstrap CI on the
advantage.

| blend | months | exSharpe (blend vs MTUM) | advantage | return diff | NW *t* (diff) | bootstrap adv 95% CI | P(adv>0) |
|---|--:|---|--:|--:|--:|---|--:|
| **50/50** | 158 | 0.924 vs 0.941 | **−0.016** | −26.4 bps/mo | **−1.88** | [−0.139, +0.164] | 0.573 |
| **inverse-vol** | 146 | 0.875 vs 0.919 | **−0.044** | −32.4 bps/mo | −1.73 | [−0.175, +0.188] | 0.524 |

**The claimed higher Sharpe does not appear.** The 50/50 advantage is **−0.016** — a
statistical wash whose bootstrap CI straddles zero (P(adv>0) = 0.57). The *return* it gives
up, by contrast, is real: **−26.4 bps/mo** (one-sample *t* = −2.21; NW *t* = −1.88), the
predictable cost of dialling down momentum's exposure. Costs are irrelevant here — at 3
bps/side and ~1%/mo turnover the net advantage (−0.017) is indistinguishable from the gross.
The inverse-vol blend, which chases the calmer sleeve harder, does slightly **worse**.

## Crash geometry — the whole point ("without the crashes")

Worst peak-to-trough drawdown inside each named window (full-window figure is the whole
158-month curve):

| window | MTUM | 50/50 blend | USMV |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| full window (158m) | −30.2% | **−22.2%** | −19.1% |
| **2020 COVID** (Jan–Jun) | −17.9% | **−18.5%** | −19.1% |
| **2022 bear** (full year) | −21.2% | **−17.7%** | −14.1% |
| 2018 Q4 | −15.4% | **−11.6%** | −7.6% |

The full-window drawdown reduction is real and mechanical (holding a lower-vol asset lowers
the peak-to-trough). But the **per-crash** protection is **inconsistent** — and it fails in
the one that matters most: in the **2020 COVID crash**, the fastest sell-off on the tape,
min-vol was **useless** and the blend drew down *slightly more than MTUM alone* (−18.5% vs
−17.9%). Min-vol helped in the slower 2022 grind and the 2018 wobble. "Defensive momentum"
is not a reliable crash hedge; it is a lower-average-volatility portfolio that sometimes,
but not always, cushions a given draw.

## Era cut — the (already absent) edge is not even stable

| era | window | months | Sharpe adv (50/50 − MTUM) | return diff | NW *t* |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| early | 2013-05 → 2019-11 | 79 | **+0.082** | −11.6 bps/mo | −1.06 |
| late | 2019-12 → 2026-06 | 79 | **−0.102** | −41.2 bps/mo | −1.62 |

The (tiny) Sharpe advantage **flips sign** across the two halves — mildly positive when
momentum was choppy (2013-19), clearly negative in the momentum-led 2020s. Not era-robust in
either magnitude or sign.

## Synthetic control — the machinery is faithful

Deterministic joint (momentum, min-vol, bench, cash) monthly world, 160 months, with a
tunable planted crash/diversification `edge` (`data.synthetic_sleeves`):

| world | Sharpe adv (blend − MTUM) | NW *t* (diff) | blend maxDD vs MTUM |
|---|--:|--:|---|
| null (edge=0, sleeves identical) | **+0.000** | — (diff exactly 0) | −27.7% vs −27.7% |
| planted (edge=1, momentum crashes) | **+0.242** | **+2.56** | **−48.0% vs −67.6%** |

On the null the two sleeves are the *same series*, so every blend is exactly a sleeve — the
advantage is precisely zero and the drawdowns are identical (no false positive). On a
planted edge — momentum takes the crashes, min-vol stays calm — the estimator recovers a
positive Sharpe advantage *and* a shallower blend drawdown. The machinery detects a real
defensive-momentum edge **when one is present**. *(Machinery proof only — never cited in
support of a stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — MIXED.** Two claims, two answers. The **vol / full-window-drawdown reduction is
  real and mechanical** (13.1% vs 16.3% vol; −22.2% vs −30.2% maxDD) — a genuine risk cut.
  But the **headline "higher Sharpe" claim is refuted**: the 50/50 excess-Sharpe advantage
  over MTUM is **−0.016**, a wash whose bootstrap CI straddles zero, whose sign **flips
  across eras**, and whose only robust component is a **significant return give-up**
  (−26 bps/mo, *t* −2.21). The blend rides the straight line between its sleeves — no
  diversification convexity. And the crash protection is **inconsistent**: min-vol *failed*
  in the 2020 COVID crash (blend drew down more than MTUM). The classic 2009 momentum crash
  the thesis rests on is **out of sample** (MTUM ETF born 2013). Real risk reduction, absent
  Sharpe edge, unreliable crash hedge → Mixed.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is nothing to bank. Costs are trivial (≈1%/mo turnover,
  3 bps/side leaves the Sharpe advantage unchanged at −0.017), so this is **not** a
  cost-erosion story — it is a **no-edge** story dressed as one. The blend's entire "benefit"
  is a **beta / volatility dial**: you hold less momentum, so you crash less *and* earn less,
  netting to the same risk-adjusted return you started with. "Momentum without the crashes"
  is really "**less momentum — less crash, less return, same Sharpe**." Anyone wanting lower
  drawdowns can dial down momentum against cash and skip the min-vol sleeve entirely. The
  apparent edge dissolves into replicable beta reduction — a Mirage.

**In one line:** blending MTUM with USMV buys a calmer ride at an almost exactly matching cut
in return — the Sharpe is a wash (−0.016, CI straddles zero), the crash protection is
unreliable (min-vol failed in 2020), and the free lunch the pitch promises isn't on the menu.
